why: Only the lightest block's and the heaviest block's positions matter: bubble the minimum to the front (its index swaps) and the maximum to the back (n-1-index swaps). If the minimum starts to the right of the maximum, one swap moves both at once, so subtract 1.
hints: The middle blocks can be in any order. Which two blocks actually need to move?
Moving the lightest block from index i to the front costs i adjacent swaps; moving the heaviest from index j to the back costs n-1-j.
Add the two costs, and if i > j subtract 1 because the two blocks cross and one swap serves both. One pass to find i and j: O(n).
pitfalls: The crossing case: in [3, 2, 1] the answer is 3, not 4.
Blocks are distinct, so the minimum and maximum are unique.
constraints:
• 2 <= n <= 10^5
  • 1 <= blocks[i] <= 10^9
  • blocks consists of distinct integers.
